## Scope and main messages

The gamma-Poisson construction behind `gsDesignNB::nb_sim()` also implies a
model for **time to the first event**. This provides a useful bridge between
negative binomial (NB) recurrent-event methods and survival analysis. It does
not make their estimands, sample-size formulas, or monitoring information
interchangeable.

This vignette develops that bridge, reproduces marginal-hazard plots, and
compares alternative models for cancer and prevention studies. The numerical
examples are illustrative, not fitted clinical data or recommended clinical
parameters. All times are in years. The calculations are analytical and require
no Monte Carlo simulation.

The central distinctions are:

1. Constant individual hazards need not produce constant population hazards.
2. A constant treatment hazard ratio conditional on frailty need not remain
   constant after averaging over survivors.
3. Changing treatment dispersion is different from applying the same
   multiplicative treatment effect to every individual's rate.
4. A useful parametric model may have a semiparametric counterpart, but not
   necessarily the simple partial likelihood and score test of Cox regression.

This is a methodological extension of the
[sample-size vignette](sample-size-nbinom.html), not an implementation of new
survival-analysis functions in `gsDesignNB`.

## Gamma frailty: recurrent counts and the first event

Let $g=C,T$ denote control and treatment. Write

$$
Z_i\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(1/k,\ \text{scale}=k),\qquad
E(Z_i)=1,\quad \operatorname{Var}(Z_i)=k,
\qquad \Lambda_{ig}=\lambda_g Z_i.
$$

For $k=0$, interpret $Z_i=1$ deterministically. Conditional on $Z_i$, assume a
homogeneous Poisson process with rate $\Lambda_{ig}$. At a fixed follow-up $t$,

$$
E\{N_g(t)\}=\lambda_g t,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}\{N_g(t)\}=\lambda_g t+k(\lambda_g t)^2.
$$

Thus $k$ is exactly the package's NB dispersion, not its reciprocal.
A distribution for counts at a single time does not by itself specify an event
process; the conditional Poisson-process assumption supplies that additional
structure. A minimum gap imposed **after** an event does not change time to the
first event, but changes the subsequent recurrent-event process.

Let $T_1$ denote time to the first event. Gamma integration gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_g(t)&=E\{\exp(-\lambda_g Z_i t)\}
       =(1+k\lambda_g t)^{-1/k},\\
h_g(t)&=-\frac{d}{dt}\log S_g(t)
       =\frac{\lambda_g}{1+k\lambda_g t},\\
E(Z_i\mid T_1>t,g)&=\frac{1}{1+k\lambda_g t}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The limits at $k=0$ are exponential survival and constant hazard. For $k>0$,
this is the Lomax (Pareto type II) survival distribution. Its hazard decreases
because high-rate individuals experience events earlier and leave the
first-event risk set, not because their individual rates decline. This is the
selection mechanism central to frailty models [@vaupel1979heterogeneity].
The unconditional recurrent-event rate remains $\lambda_g$ when observation
continues after events under the same process.

There is direct literature on this connection: @siri2012firstevent developed
an NB-derived first-event regression model and applied it to multiple sclerosis
relapses. @claggett2018comparison studied first-event and recurrent-event
analyses in cardiovascular trials, including attenuation of Cox estimates
relative to a common patient-level effect under risk heterogeneity. Their
comparisons also show why conclusions about power depend on assumptions such
as treatment discontinuation after an event.

### Constant conditional effects, changing marginal effects

With a common $k$ and $\lambda_T=r\lambda_C$, the same-frailty conditional
treatment hazard ratio is $r$. The marginal hazard ratio is instead

$$
\operatorname{HR}_m(t)
=r\frac{1+k\lambda_Ct}{1+kr\lambda_Ct}.
$$

For $r<1$ and $k>0$, it increases from $r$ toward 1. In contrast,
$S_T(t)=S_C(rt)$: this particular marginal model is also accelerated failure
time (AFT), with treatment multiplying survival-time quantiles by $1/r$.
That AFT interpretation is specific to the time structure; conditional PH
with an arbitrary baseline does not generally imply marginal AFT.

On a log-hazard axis, a constant marginal hazard ratio would appear as a
constant **vertical separation**. The curves need not be straight.

```{r plot-helpers}
# Local vignette helpers; no new exported package functions.
gamma_survival <- function(H, k) {
  if (k == 0) exp(-H) else exp(-log1p(k * H) / k)
}
gamma_hazard <- function(h, H, k) h / (1 + k * H)

arm_levels <- c("Control", "Treatment r = 0.7", "Treatment r = 0.5")
arm_colours <- setNames(c("#223C57", "#078477", "#C46723"), arm_levels)
arm_lines <- setNames(c("solid", "longdash", "dotdash"), arm_levels)
plot_style <- list(
  scale_colour_manual(values = arm_colours),
  scale_linetype_manual(values = arm_lines),
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11),
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom", legend.title = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
)

common <- expand.grid(
  time = seq(0, 5, length.out = 301),
  k = c(0, 0.5, 1), r = c(1, 0.7, 0.5)
)
common$arm <- factor(common$r, levels = c(1, 0.7, 0.5),
                     labels = arm_levels)
common$panel <- factor(common$k, labels = c("k = 0", "k = 0.5", "k = 1"))
common$hazard <- with(common, gamma_hazard(r, r * time, k))
common$hr <- with(common, hazard / gamma_hazard(1, time, k))
```

```{r common-dispersion, fig.cap="Common gamma dispersion. Control mean individual rate is 1/year; treatment mean rates are 0.7 and 0.5/year. Equal scales are used across panels."}
ggplot(common, aes(time, hazard, colour = arm, linetype = arm)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, nrow = 1) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(0.15, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Time (years)", y = "Marginal hazard (/year; log scale)") +
  plot_style
```

### A first-event likelihood that resembles NB regression

For independent right censoring, observe $X_i=\min(T_{1i},C_i)>0$ and
$\delta_i=I(T_{1i}\le C_i)$. Omitting the censoring likelihood,

$$
L_i(\lambda_i,k)
=h_i(X_i)^{\delta_i}S_i(X_i)
=\lambda_i^{\delta_i}
 (1+k\lambda_iX_i)^{-1/k-\delta_i}.
$$

An NB mass at $y_i=\delta_i\in\{0,1\}$ with mean $\lambda_iX_i$ equals this
likelihood times $X_i^{\delta_i}$. That factor is parameter-free. Consequently,
an NB likelihood with an offset $\log X_i$ can reproduce this parametric
first-event likelihood, including its dependence on $k$.

This is a **likelihood identity**, not a claim that the binary indicator is NB
conditional on its event-dependent exposure. Exposure must stop at the first
event. Plugging the binary indicator into an NB model with full administrative
follow-up is a different analysis. Moreover, fixed-exposure NB information,
software diagnostics, and recurrent-event group sequential calibrations do not
automatically transfer to this observation scheme.

In particular, equal likelihood maximizers do not justify blindly reusing
fixed-exposure GLM standard errors. For $\eta_i=\log\lambda_i$ and
$\mu_i=\lambda_iX_i$, the observed first-event information for $\eta_i$,
holding $k$ fixed, is

$$
J_{\eta_i\eta_i}
=\frac{\mu_i(1+k\delta_i)}{(1+k\mu_i)^2},
$$

whereas the fixed-exposure NB GLM weight is $\mu_i/(1+k\mu_i)$.
Use the appropriate first-event likelihood information; if $k$ is estimated,
its nuisance-parameter contribution must also be included.

## Treatment changes the dispersion as well as the mean

Now allow

$$
\Lambda_g\sim\operatorname{Gamma}
 \left(1/k_g,\ \text{scale}=k_g\lambda_g\right),\quad
\operatorname{Var}(\Lambda_g)=k_g\lambda_g^2.
$$

The resulting expressions are

$$
h_g(t)=\frac{\lambda_g}{1+k_g\lambda_g t},\qquad
\operatorname{HR}_m(t)
=r\frac{1+k_C\lambda_Ct}{1+k_T r\lambda_Ct}.
$$

Here $r=\lambda_T/\lambda_C$ is the ratio of **mean underlying individual
rates**, also the initial marginal hazard ratio. It is no longer a common
individual treatment HR. Two arm-specific rate distributions alone do not
specify paired individual potential outcomes or who benefits.

The following three-by-three display retains $\lambda_C=1$/year and
$k_C=0,0.5,1$ across columns. Rows set $k_T=fk_C$ for $f=1,0.5,0.2$:
no, moderate (50%), and high (80%) reduction in normalized frailty variance.
For $k_C>0$, the absolute rate-variance ratio is $fr^2$, not $f$.

```{r dispersion-data}
impact <- expand.grid(
  time = seq(0, 5, length.out = 301),
  kC = c(0, 0.5, 1), f = c(1, 0.5, 0.2), r = c(1, 0.7, 0.5)
)
impact$k_arm <- with(impact, ifelse(r == 1, kC, f * kC))
impact$hazard <- with(impact, gamma_hazard(r, r * time, k_arm))
impact$hr <- with(impact, hazard / gamma_hazard(1, time, kC))
impact$arm <- factor(impact$r, levels = c(1, 0.7, 0.5), labels = arm_levels)
impact$control <- factor(
  impact$kC, levels = c(0, 0.5, 1),
  labels = c("Control k = 0", "Control k = 0.5", "Control k = 1")
)
impact$change <- factor(
  impact$f, levels = c(1, 0.5, 0.2),
  labels = c("No reduction", "50% reduction", "80% reduction")
)
```

```{r dispersion-hazards, fig.height=7, fig.cap="Treatment changes normalized frailty dispersion. The control curve is unchanged down each column. All panels share the same axes; the zero-dispersion column repeats because multiplying zero dispersion still gives zero."}
ggplot(impact, aes(time, hazard, colour = arm, linetype = arm)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_grid(change ~ control) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(0.15, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Time (years)", y = "Marginal hazard (/year; log scale)") +
  plot_style
```

```{r dispersion-ratios, fig.height=7, fig.cap="Marginal hazard ratios for the same scenarios. The dotted horizontal line denotes equal hazards, not equal survival probabilities."}
ggplot(subset(impact, r < 1),
       aes(time, hr, colour = arm, linetype = arm)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_grid(change ~ control) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(0.5, 0.7, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5)) +
  labs(x = "Time (years)", y = "Marginal treatment/control HR (log scale)") +
  plot_style
```

For positive $k_C,k_T$, the limiting HR is $k_C/k_T$. If $r<1$ and
$k_T<k_C$, the marginal HR crosses 1 at

$$
t_{\rm cross}=\frac{1-r}{r\lambda_C(k_C-k_T)}.
$$

For example, $r=0.7$, $k_C=1$, and $k_T=0.5$ give a crossing at about
0.86 years. This is not treatment wearing off within a patient: every
individual rate in this example is constant. A hazard crossing does not
identify a survival-curve crossing. For $r<1$ and $k_T<k_C$ here, survival
ordering eventually reverses too, later than the hazard crossing and possibly
far beyond the observed follow-up.
Late hazards should always be interpreted alongside survival and numbers
remaining at risk.

The direction of dispersion change is a scientific assumption, not a default
property of treatment. If treatment increases dispersion, then

$$
\operatorname{sign}\{\operatorname{HR}_m'(t)\}
=\operatorname{sign}(k_C-rk_T).
$$

In particular, $k_T=k_C/r$ gives a constant marginal HR $r$ despite different
dispersion; $k_T>k_C/r$ makes the HR decrease. If $k_T=0<k_C$, treatment has
constant marginal hazard and the HR grows without bound. The zero-dispersion
limits must therefore be handled separately from the ratio $k_C/k_T$.

## Which marginal hazard shapes are possible?

### Why exponential mixtures cannot produce a hump

For any mixture of fixed nonnegative exponential rates, where the required
moments exist,

$$
h_m(t)=E(\Lambda\mid T_1>t),\qquad
h_m'(t)=-\operatorname{Var}(\Lambda\mid T_1>t)\le0.
$$

Thus changing the mixing distribution cannot make a fixed-exponential-rate
mixture increase and then decrease. To obtain that shape, allow individual
hazards to change over time, or use a different survival model.

### A time-varying baseline with gamma frailty

Let $h(t\mid Z,r)=Zr h_0(t)$ and $H_0(t)=\int_0^t h_0(u)\,du$. Then

$$
S_r(t)=\{1+krH_0(t)\}^{-1/k},\qquad
h_{m,r}(t)=\frac{r h_0(t)}{1+krH_0(t)}.
$$

For $r=1$,

$$
h_m'(t)=
\frac{h_0'(t)\{1+kH_0(t)\}-k h_0(t)^2}
     {\{1+kH_0(t)\}^2}.
$$

The numerator separates increasing within-person risk from depletion of
high-risk individuals. Three instructive examples are:

| Individual baseline | Marginal behavior under gamma frailty |
|:--|:--|
| Exponential: $h_0(t)=a$ | Decreases for $k>0$; constant for $k=0$. |
| Weibull: $H_0(t)=at^p$ | For $p>1,k>0$, rises then falls, peaking at $\{(p-1)/(ka)\}^{1/p}$. With $k=0$ it keeps increasing. |
| Gompertz: $h_0(t)=ae^{bt}$, $b>0$ | For $k>0$, increases if $b>ka$, is constant if $b=ka$, and decreases if $b<ka$; its limit is $b/k$. |

The Weibull-gamma marginal survival $(1+kat^p)^{-1/k}$ is a Burr-type
distribution; at $k=1$ it is log-logistic. Gamma-Gompertz mortality
deceleration is discussed by @bohnstedt2021deceleration. Notably, an
exponentially growing individual hazard gives a plateau, not automatically
a marginal downturn.

The next example uses baselines with a common initial hazard of 1/year:
constant, linear increasing, and Gompertz increasing. The linear baseline
provides a nonzero starting hazard and a subsequent marginal peak.

```{r shape-data}
shapes <- expand.grid(
  time = seq(0, 5, length.out = 401), r = c(1, 0.7, 0.5),
  shape = c("Constant", "Linear increase", "Gompertz increase")
)
shapes$h0 <- with(shapes, ifelse(
  shape == "Constant", 1,
  ifelse(shape == "Linear increase", 1 + 2 * time, exp(time))
))
shapes$H0 <- with(shapes, ifelse(
  shape == "Constant", time,
  ifelse(shape == "Linear increase", time + time^2, expm1(time))
))
shapes$hazard <- with(shapes, gamma_hazard(r * h0, r * H0, 0.5))
shapes$arm <- factor(shapes$r, levels = c(1, 0.7, 0.5), labels = arm_levels)
```

```{r hazard-shapes, fig.cap="Three marginal shapes from different individual baselines, all with k = 0.5 and initial control hazard 1/year. These are illustrative mathematical models."}
ggplot(shapes, aes(time, hazard, colour = arm, linetype = arm)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~shape, nrow = 1) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(0.15, 0.3, 0.5, 1, 2)) +
  labs(x = "Time (years)", y = "Marginal hazard (/year; log scale)") +
  plot_style
```

## Biological interpretation in cancer

Two selection processes should not be conflated. Chemotherapy can remove
sensitive cells while resistant subclones persist and expand **within a
patient**. Separately, patients with faster progression leave the
progression-free risk set earlier, changing its composition **across
patients**. Genomic evidence for treatment-associated clonal selection includes
paired acute myeloid leukaemia diagnosis/relapse samples [@ding2012clonal] and
single-cell studies of triple-negative breast cancer during neoadjuvant
chemotherapy [@kim2018chemoresistance].

These observations motivate, but do not uniquely identify, the following
phenomenological model for low initial progression risk followed by regrowth:

$$
q(t)=\epsilon+b(t-\tau)_+,\qquad
Q(t)=\epsilon t+\frac b2(t-\tau)_+^2,\qquad
h_m(t)=\frac{q(t)}{1+kQ(t)}.
$$

Here $\tau$ is a modeled delay and $b$ is a rate of increase in the individual
baseline hazard, not a directly measured clone growth rate. After $\tau$, the
marginal hazard initially rises if
$b(1+k\epsilon\tau)>k\epsilon^2$. It ultimately decreases as $2/(kt)$ for
$k>0$, even though every individual hazard $Zq(t)$ keeps increasing.

```{r cancer-example, fig.cap="An illustrative post-treatment progression model: epsilon = 0.1/year, delay = 1 year, slope = 0.5/year squared, k = 0.5. Rising individual risk and falling marginal risk can coexist. The right panel exposes how few patients remain progression-free late."}
cancer <- data.frame(time = seq(0, 10, length.out = 501))
cancer$q <- with(cancer, 0.1 + 0.5 * pmax(time - 1, 0))
cancer$Q <- with(cancer, 0.1 * time + 0.25 * pmax(time - 1, 0)^2)
cancer$hazard <- with(cancer, gamma_hazard(q, Q, 0.5))
cancer$survival <- gamma_survival(cancer$Q, 0.5)
par_old <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(cancer$time, cancer$q, type = "l", log = "y", col = "#223C57",
     xlab = "Time (years)", ylab = "Hazard (/year; log scale)", lwd = 2)
lines(cancer$time, cancer$hazard, col = "#078477", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("topleft", c("Individual, Z = 1", "Marginal"),
       col = c("#223C57", "#078477"), lty = c(1, 2), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
plot(cancer$time, cancer$survival, type = "l", col = "#078477", lwd = 2,
     ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Time (years)", ylab = "Progression-free probability")
par(par_old)
```

This is not a clone-level mechanistic model or proof that a fitted hump is
caused by resistance. Longitudinal tumor burden, circulating tumor DNA,
resistance markers, and treatment history would help distinguish mechanisms.
If drug activity genuinely wanes, allow an arm-specific baseline $q_g(t)$ or
time-varying individual effect $r(t)$. The cumulative treatment hazard must then
use $\int_0^t r(u)q_C(u)\,du$, not $r(t)Q_C(t)$.

Also, $h_m(t)\to0$ does **not** imply cure: in this example $Q(t)\to\infty$
and $S(t)\to0$. Durable cure requires a different structural assumption.
Progression-specific hazards, progression-free survival (which often includes
death), and overall survival are different endpoints. A death competing with
progression is not simply independent loss to follow-up; background mortality
must also be considered before interpreting a late decline as cure.

## Other parametric survival models

An arm-specific distribution is a convenient statistical description; its
parameters need not correspond to biological compartments. The following
families are useful starting points, with $a,p,b>0$ and
$z=(\log t-\mu)/\sigma$.

| Model | Survival or hazard | Shapes and treatment interpretation |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Exponential | $S(t)=e^{-at}$ | Constant hazard. A rate ratio is also a PH effect; a time ratio gives an AFT interpretation. |
| Weibull | $S(t)=e^{-at^p}$ | Increasing for $p>1$, constant for $p=1$, decreasing for $p<1$. Common shape gives both PH and AFT representations; arm-specific shapes allow non-PH. |
| Gompertz | $h(t)=ae^{bt}$ | Increasing for $b>0$; useful for increasing age-related risk. Gamma mixing can produce deceleration or a plateau. |
| Log-logistic | $S(t)=(1+at^p)^{-1}$ | Decreasing hazard for $p\le1$, hump-shaped for $p>1$. Common shape gives AFT and proportional event odds, not generally PH. |
| Lognormal | $S(t)=1-\Phi(z)$, $h(t)=\phi(z)/\{\sigma t[1-\Phi(z)]\}$ | A hump-shaped hazard; a common log-time scale gives AFT. No frailty mixture is required. |
| Generalized gamma | A flexible family containing Weibull, gamma, and lognormal cases/limits | Separates location, scale, and shape; permits a broader range of hazards and sensitivity analyses [@prentice1974loggamma]. |
| Piecewise exponential | $h_g(t)=a_{gj}$ in prespecified intervals | Transparent delayed or waning effects; requires choices of cutpoints and treatment contrasts. |
| Flexible parametric splines | For example, $\log H_g(t)=s(\log t)+\beta g+g\,s_T(\log t)$ | Smooth baseline and time-varying effects; $s_T=0$ is PH on this scale [@royston2002flexible]. |

For log-logistic survival, event odds $(1-S)/S=at^p$. For lognormal and
generalized gamma models, the AFT interpretation requires common non-location
parameters across arms. Freeing shape or scale trades a simple treatment
summary for greater flexibility. Likewise, spline models with a fixed finite
number of coefficients are **flexible parametric**, not automatically
semiparametric Cox models.

Royston--Parmar models allow modeling on cumulative-hazard, odds, or other
transformation scales; their original paper includes prognostic modeling and
treatment-effect estimation. Smooth fit within follow-up is not assurance of
correct extrapolation beyond it. Tail behavior, especially a cure fraction,
should be checked against clinical knowledge and follow-up support.

### Cancer: cure versus postponement

A mixture-cure model explicitly separates a fraction $\pi_g$ that will never
experience the specified cancer event from the susceptible distribution:

$$
S_g(t)=\pi_g+(1-\pi_g)S_{u,g}(t),\qquad
h_g(t)=\frac{(1-\pi_g)S_{u,g}(t)h_{u,g}(t)}
                  {\pi_g+(1-\pi_g)S_{u,g}(t)}.
$$

Boag's early cancer work is a foundational example [@boag1949cure].
@gamel1994adjuvant fitted parametric models, including lognormal models, to
five adjuvant breast-cancer trials to distinguish estimated cure probabilities
from recurrence-free time among uncured patients. These are model-dependent
distinctions between preventing and postponing recurrence.

Short follow-up can make a cure fraction difficult to distinguish from a
long susceptible tail. Cure from a cancer event does not mean immortality:
overall survival must include other-cause mortality. If $S_u$ specifically
models cancer-related death among uncured patients, with independent
background survival $S_b(t)$, an illustrative overall-survival formulation is
$S_{\rm overall}(t)=S_b(t)\{\pi+(1-\pi)S_u(t)\}$, whose overall hazard adds
background mortality to the mixture's cancer-death hazard. If $S_u$ instead
models recurrence, this product describes recurrence-or-death-free survival,
not overall survival.

### Lipid lowering and cardiovascular prevention

A useful actual parametric application is @yourman2021statins: their
meta-analysis fitted Weibull survival curves to annual arm-level event data
from eight statin primary-prevention trials, allowing shape and scale to
differ between arms. They estimated the follow-up required to reach specified
absolute risk-reduction thresholds. This was a parametric reanalysis, not
necessarily the analysis model used by each original trial.

An increasing absolute benefit over time is not itself evidence of a delayed
biological onset. Even an immediate constant HR $r<1$ produces

$$
S_T(t)-S_C(t)=e^{-rH_C(t)}-e^{-H_C(t)},
$$

which starts at zero and initially grows. A threshold-based "time to benefit"
and a treatment-effect lag are therefore different quantities.
If a genuine lag, gradual benefit, or waning is scientifically plausible,
piecewise effects, splines, or arm-specific Weibull shapes provide
sensitivity models. For example,

$$
h_T(t)=r(t)h_C(t),\qquad
r(t)=
\begin{cases}
1,&t<\tau,\\
r_\infty,&t\ge\tau,
\end{cases}
$$

is an explicit delayed-effect assumption, not something implied by a
Weibull distribution or by a positive time-to-benefit estimate. Smooth
alternatives can avoid a discontinuous onset.

### Infection prevention: exposure, response, and waning

In an infection-prevention study, an illustrative conditional hazard is

$$
h_i(t)=Z_i\,\lambda_{\rm exposure}(c_i+t)\{1-\operatorname{VE}_i(t)\},
$$

where $c_i$ is calendar time of entry and $t$ is time since vaccination.
Calendar-time force of infection, time since vaccination, and individual
exposure/susceptibility are different components.

For homogeneous exposure with cumulative hazard $B(t)$, compare two idealized
vaccines having protection $e$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_{\rm leaky}(t)&=\exp\{-(1-e)B(t)\},\\
S_{\rm all\ or\ none}(t)&=e+(1-e)\exp\{-B(t)\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The first reduces everyone's infection hazard by the same fraction. The
second completely protects fraction $e$ and leaves the remainder unchanged.
They have the same initial average hazard reduction, but different later
risk sets. Permanent protection in the second expression is an explicit
idealization; waning protection needs additional structure.

@longini1996vaccine developed a frailty-mixture model with heterogeneous
response and a mass at zero, applying it to measles-outbreak data.
@white2010heterogeneity distinguished exposure heterogeneity, heterogeneous
vaccine responses, and true waning in malaria-vaccine efficacy interpretation.
An increasing marginal HR can reflect depletion of susceptible controls even
when individual vaccine protection is unchanged.

For a more biological parametric example, @white2015vaccine linked a biphasic
antibody-decay model to protection and event-time analyses in an RTS,S malaria
vaccine trial, accounting for exposure and immunity. The exponential
components described **antibody decay**, not exponentially distributed event
times. First infection, first clinical disease, and recurrent infections also
require distinct endpoint definitions.

## Anderson's VLDAFT model

The reference is **Keaven M. Anderson (1991), Biometrics 47(1), 281--288,
"A nonproportional hazards Weibull accelerated failure time regression model"**
[@anderson1991vldaft]. It analyzed Framingham heart-disease incidence over
32 years using risk factors measured before age 50. The model allowed
log-time dispersion to depend on location and was estimated by maximum
likelihood.

VLDAFT denotes **varying location and dispersion accelerated failure time**.
Using the explicit restatement in @mannan2010weibull, its linked
location--dispersion formulation is

$$
\log T_i=\mu_i+\sigma_i\varepsilon_i,\qquad
\mu_i=x_i^\top\beta,\qquad
\log\sigma_i=\theta_0+\theta_1\mu_i,
$$

where $\varepsilon_i$ has minimum extreme-value distribution,
$F_\varepsilon(u)=1-\exp\{-\exp(u)\}$. Thus

$$
S_i(t)=\exp\left[-\exp\left\{\frac{\log t-\mu_i}{\sigma_i}\right\}\right].
$$

Here $\sigma_i$ is **log-time dispersion**, not gamma frailty variance $k$.
The Weibull shape is $p_i=1/\sigma_i$ and time scale is
$\eta_i=\exp(\mu_i)$. The link above is more restrictive than separately
modeling $\log\sigma_i=z_i^\top\gamma$.

The following consequences are obtained directly from this survival function:

$$
h_i(t)=\frac{1}{\sigma_i}e^{-\mu_i/\sigma_i}t^{1/\sigma_i-1},\qquad
\operatorname{HR}_{1:0}(t)=
\frac{\sigma_0}{\sigma_1}
e^{-\mu_1/\sigma_1+\mu_0/\sigma_0}
t^{1/\sigma_1-1/\sigma_0}.
$$

With constant $\sigma$, ordinary Weibull AFT and PH coincide. With different
$\sigma$ values, the log HR is linear in log time, and the quantile ratio is

$$
\frac{Q_1(u)}{Q_0(u)}
=e^{\mu_1-\mu_0}\{-\log(1-u)\}^{\sigma_1-\sigma_0},
\qquad 0<u<1.
$$

Hence the name does not imply a single constant acceleration factor when
dispersion varies. Each profile-specific Weibull hazard is still monotone;
the original VLDAFT model does not itself produce a hump.
Unequal-shape Weibull HRs can move toward 1 over a follow-up interval and
cross it, but their infinite-time limit is 0 or infinity, not generally 1.
This differs from common-shape gamma-frailty attenuation.

```{r vldaft-example, fig.cap="Illustrative Weibull location/dispersion effects, not estimates from Anderson's Framingham analysis. Control has time scale 2 and shape 2. Both treatment scenarios have time scale 3; fixed log-time dispersion keeps shape 2, while the linked VLDAFT example has shape 3."}
vldaft <- data.frame(time = seq(0.05, 8, length.out = 401))
vldaft$control <- dweibull(vldaft$time, shape = 2, scale = 2) /
  pweibull(vldaft$time, shape = 2, scale = 2, lower.tail = FALSE)
vldaft$fixed <- (2 / 3) * (vldaft$time / 3)
vldaft$linked <- (3 / 3) * (vldaft$time / 3)^2
# Linked example: mu_C = log(2), mu_T = log(3),
# theta_0 = 0, theta_1 = -1, so sigma = exp(-mu).
par_old <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
matplot(vldaft$time, vldaft[c("control", "fixed", "linked")],
        type = "l", log = "y", lty = c(1, 2, 3), lwd = 2,
        col = c("#223C57", "#078477", "#C46723"),
        xlab = "Time (years)", ylab = "Hazard (/year; log scale)")
legend("bottomright", c("Control", "Fixed dispersion", "Linked dispersion"),
       col = c("#223C57", "#078477", "#C46723"),
       lty = c(1, 2, 3), lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
matplot(vldaft$time, vldaft[c("fixed", "linked")] / vldaft$control,
        type = "l", log = "y", lty = c(2, 3), lwd = 2,
        col = c("#078477", "#C46723"),
        xlab = "Time (years)", ylab = "Treatment/control HR (log scale)")
abline(h = 1, lty = 3, col = "grey50")
par(par_old)
```

One possible extension is to add gamma frailty to these Weibull individual
hazards. Writing $H_i(t)=A_it^{p_i}$, where
$A_i=e^{-p_i\mu_i}$, gives

$$
h_{m,i}(t)=\frac{p_iA_it^{p_i-1}}{1+kA_it^{p_i}}.
$$

For $p_i>1,k>0$ this is hump-shaped. With common positive $k$, its late
hazard ratio tends to $p_1/p_0$, not necessarily 1. This is a
**derived frailty extension**, not an attribution to Anderson's original
model.

## Semiparametric modeling and testing

### What is analogous to Cox regression?

Cox's model leaves the baseline hazard unspecified while estimating a
constant log HR through partial likelihood [@cox1972regression]. For a
two-arm comparison without tied event times, its score test at zero treatment
effect is the ordinary logrank test. Let $A=1$ denote treatment and $A=0$ control.
Several alternatives also leave a
baseline distribution unspecified, but differ in treatment interpretation and
estimation:

| Framework | Unspecified component and treatment parameter | Inference route |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Cox PH: $h(t\mid A)=h_0(t)e^{\beta A}$ | Baseline hazard; constant log HR $\beta$ | Partial likelihood; score/logrank, Wald, or likelihood-ratio inference |
| Gamma transformation / generalized odds-rate | Baseline cumulative hazard; effect on transformed survival | Semiparametric likelihood or estimating equations; requires a specified or identifiable link |
| AFT: $\log T=\alpha+\beta A+\varepsilon$ | Error distribution; constant log time ratio | Censored rank estimating equations and resampling [@jin2003rank] |
| Location--scale AFT extension | Error distribution; effects on log-time location and dispersion | Joint rank equations and joint/component tests [@burke2020multiparameter] |
| Time-varying additive hazards: $h(t\mid A)=\alpha_0(t)+A\alpha_1(t)$ | Baseline and coefficient functions; instantaneous hazard difference | Estimating equations for cumulative coefficients [@aalen1989linear] |

For binary treatment alone, time-varying additive hazards can represent any
two arm hazards by setting $\alpha_0=h_C$ and $\alpha_1=h_T-h_C$.
A constant additive coefficient would impose a much stronger restriction.
General covariate models must still respect nonnegative hazards.

### A direct gamma-frailty transformation model

Define

$$
G_k(s)=
\begin{cases}
(s^{-k}-1)/k,&k>0,\\
-\log s,&k=0.
\end{cases}
$$

The gamma-frailty model with common dispersion and an unspecified baseline satisfies

$$
G_k\{S(t\mid A)\}=e^{\beta A}H_0(t).
$$

Thus $k=0$ gives PH, $k=1$ gives proportional **failure odds** $(1-S)/S$,
and other fixed values give a transformation model. Semiparametric frailty
inference with an unspecified baseline has an established literature
[@kosorok2004frailty]. @choi2012transformation also allow transformation-link
parameters to depend on covariates, making it a particularly relevant
starting point for treatment effects on dispersion.

However, estimating both an unrestricted baseline and frailty parameters
requires identification checks. With no covariate effect, any common $k$
can be absorbed into
$H_0^{(k)}(t)=G_k\{S(t)\}$. The common variance is then unidentified.
@song2009identifiability explicitly treat this nonstandard testing problem.
It is not resolved simply by using a more flexible optimizer.

Arm-specific dispersion adds another possible nonidentifiability: when
$k_T r=k_C$, a continuum of frailty/baseline specifications can yield the
same PH pair of marginal survival curves. A covariate-dependent link is
therefore a promising framework, not an automatic identifiable fit for
arbitrary two-arm data. In contrast, fixing the conditional baseline to
be exponential imposes the parametric structure that identifies each arm's
Lomax distribution parameters.

The boundary $k=0$ is a separate issue. Standard chi-square likelihood-ratio
calibration should not be assumed for variance-component tests
[@self1987nonstandard]. Even the familiar one-variance-component mixture
reference requires appropriate regularity; it does not automatically apply
to joint dispersion tests or unidentified nuisance parameters.

### A semiparametric counterpart to VLDAFT already exists

@burke2020multiparameter develop a location--scale model for log survival
time with a completely unspecified common error distribution, covariates
in both location and scale, and joint rank-based estimating equations.
The paper provides resampling-based uncertainty estimates and component
and joint tests; its application uses observational lung-cancer data.

With reference location and scale normalized to identify the error
distribution, treatment can enter as

$$
\log T=\beta A+\exp(\gamma A)\varepsilon.
$$

Under the paper's regularity conditions, testing $\gamma=0$ assesses
constant acceleration, and jointly testing $(\beta,\gamma)=(0,0)$ assesses
both treatment components. This is a close analogue of "model plus
corresponding test," although not Cox partial likelihood or a single
ordinary logrank statistic.

In an unspecified-error model, constant dispersion implies AFT, **not**
generally PH. For Weibull event times (minimum extreme-value log-time errors),
constant dispersion also gives PH.
Also, fitting free location and scale intercepts alongside an unrestricted
error distribution would require additional normalization.
Anderson's linked specification introduces its own issue in a treatment-only
model: when the treatment location contrast is zero, the linking slope
$\theta_1$ cannot be separately learned from the common scale. Separate
treatment coefficients in location and log scale give a clearer joint
treatment-testing formulation.

The distinction from gamma mixing remains important: a location--scale
model describes a distribution of log event times, while a frailty model
specifies latent hazards. One need not have the other model's biological
interpretation.

### Logrank validity, weights, and the null being tested

Non-PH under the alternative does **not** invalidate the ordinary logrank
test of equal survival curves under independent censoring. It changes power;
crossing hazards can make contributions cancel. A single fitted Cox
hazard ratio under non-PH does not describe the instantaneous HR throughout follow-up, and a
robust covariance estimate does not restore proportional hazards
[@lin1989robust].

For the gamma model with prespecified common $k$, differentiating the marginal log HR at
$\beta=\log r=0$ gives

$$
\log\operatorname{HR}_m(t)
\simeq \frac{\beta}{1+kH_0(t)}
=\beta S_0(t)^k.
$$

This gives a local-efficiency motivation for an early-weighted
Fleming--Harrington statistic with
$w(t)=\widehat S_{\rm pooled}(t-)^k$, the FH$(k,0)$ weight
[@harrington1982rank]. It is not a guarantee of best power, particularly
when treatment changes dispersion or effects are delayed.
Weights should be prespecified, or selection/combination should be
calibrated; choosing the smallest observed $p$-value across weights is
not valid without adjustment. Equality of survival curves is also different
from a one-sided null that treatment survival is nowhere better; weighted
tests require care about that distinction [@magirr2019weighted].

The estimand matters even more if $k_T\ne k_C$. Setting $r=1$ then does
not make survival curves equal. A logrank rejection can indicate a first-event
distribution difference without any difference in the mean individual rate.
In the parametric two-arm gamma-exponential model, the equal-survival null is
$r=1$ **and** $k_T=k_C$, not just equality of mean rates.

### Model-light treatment summaries

Kaplan--Meier survival probabilities at prespecified times and restricted
mean survival time (RMST) offer interpretable marginal contrasts without PH:

$$
\Delta_{\rm RMST}(\tau)
=\int_0^\tau\{S_T(t)-S_C(t)\}\,dt.
$$

RMST measures additional event-free time through a chosen horizon, not a
latent rate ratio [@royston2013rmst]. Choose $\tau$ before examining treatment
differences and within adequate follow-up support. A zero RMST difference
is not equivalent to equal survival curves, and crossing curves can cancel
in the integral as well. Competing-risk endpoints require corresponding
cumulative-incidence or restricted-time estimands, rather than treating a
competing event as ordinary censoring in Kaplan--Meier.

## Implications for gsDesignNB and future work

The package's existing NB workflows answer recurrent-event rate questions.
The first-event bridge offers useful simulation scenarios and sensitivity
analyses, but does not yet provide a validated first-event design engine.
In particular:

- Specify whether the estimand is a recurrent-event rate ratio, conditional
  hazard ratio, time ratio, survival difference, or restricted mean
  event-free time difference.
- Separate changes in mean rate, dispersion, baseline time trend, and
  treatment activity. Similar-looking hazards can arise from different
  assumptions and imply different estimands.
- Use survival curves and risk-set sizes alongside hazards; late hazards
  can be unstable or scientifically unrepresentative of the original population.
- For a new test or adaptive design, derive its information and validate
  Type I error, power, censoring sensitivity, and monitoring behavior under
  the actual observation scheme. Reusing NB count information is not enough.

An immediately useful extension would be a **scenario-generation layer**:
gamma-exponential, gamma-Weibull, arm-specific dispersion, delayed/waning
piecewise effects, and cure sensitivity. It could compare prespecified
logrank/weighted-logrank analyses with model-based and restricted-mean
analyses before adding a specialized design formula.

## Reproducibility checks

The following inexpensive checks run when this vignette is built. They verify
the zero-dispersion limit, survival derivatives, numerical gamma mixing,
the first-event/NB likelihood identity, and hazard-ratio crossing times.
They are mathematical checks, not clinical validation.

```{r mathematical-checks}
stopifnot(
  max(abs(gamma_survival(c(0, 0.2, 2), 0) -
            exp(-c(0, 0.2, 2)))) < 1e-12,
  max(abs(gamma_survival(c(0.2, 2), 1e-8) -
            exp(-c(0.2, 2)))) < 1e-8,
  all(common$hazard[common$k == 0] == common$r[common$k == 0])
)

checks <- expand.grid(k = c(0.2, 0.5, 1, 2),
                      lambda = c(0.4, 1, 2), time = c(0.1, 1, 3))
for (j in seq_len(nrow(checks))) {
  k <- checks$k[j]
  lambda <- checks$lambda[j]
  time <- checks$time[j]
  integrated <- integrate(
    function(z) exp(-lambda * time * z) *
      dgamma(z, shape = 1 / k, scale = k),
    lower = 0, upper = Inf, rel.tol = 1e-9
  )$value
  stopifnot(abs(integrated - gamma_survival(lambda * time, k)) < 1e-8)
  delta <- c(0, 1)
  loglik <- delta * log(lambda) -
    (1 / k + delta) * log1p(k * lambda * time)
  nb_loglik <- dnbinom(delta, size = 1 / k, mu = lambda * time, log = TRUE)
  stopifnot(max(abs(nb_loglik - loglik - delta * log(time))) < 1e-10)
  eps <- 1e-5
  derivative <- -(
    log(gamma_survival(lambda * (time + eps), k)) -
      log(gamma_survival(lambda * (time - eps), k))
  ) / (2 * eps)
  stopifnot(abs(derivative - gamma_hazard(lambda, lambda * time, k)) < 1e-8)
}

crossings <- expand.grid(kC = c(0.5, 1), f = c(0.5, 0.2), r = c(0.7, 0.5))
crossings$kT <- with(crossings, f * kC)
crossings$time <- with(crossings, (1 - r) / (r * (kC - kT)))
crossing_hr <- with(crossings, r * (1 + kC * time) / (1 + kT * r * time))
stopifnot(max(abs(crossing_hr - 1)) < 1e-12)

# Gamma-Weibull peak and the increasing gamma-Gompertz example.
p <- 2
a <- 0.4
k <- 0.5
peak <- ((p - 1) / (k * a))^(1 / p)
weibull_marginal <- function(t) {
  gamma_hazard(p * a * t^(p - 1), a * t^p, k)
}
stopifnot(
  weibull_marginal(peak) > weibull_marginal(peak - 0.01),
  weibull_marginal(peak) > weibull_marginal(peak + 0.01)
)
gompertz <- subset(shapes, shape == "Gompertz increase" & r == 1)
stopifnot(all(diff(gompertz$hazard) > 0), max(gompertz$hazard) < 2)

# VLDAFT parameterization, time-varying HR, and survival quantiles.
mu <- log(c(2, 3))
sigma <- exp(-mu)
time <- c(0.1, 1, 4.5, 8)
vldaft_survival <- function(t, mu, sigma) {
  exp(-exp((log(t) - mu) / sigma))
}
for (j in seq_along(mu)) {
  stopifnot(max(abs(
    vldaft_survival(time, mu[j], sigma[j]) -
      pweibull(time, shape = 1 / sigma[j], scale = exp(mu[j]),
               lower.tail = FALSE)
  )) < 1e-12)
}
hr_vldaft <- sigma[1] / sigma[2] *
  exp(-mu[2] / sigma[2] + mu[1] / sigma[1]) *
  time^(1 / sigma[2] - 1 / sigma[1])
stopifnot(max(abs(hr_vldaft - 2 * time / 9)) < 1e-12)
probs <- c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9)
qr <- qweibull(probs, shape = 3, scale = 3) /
  qweibull(probs, shape = 2, scale = 2)
stopifnot(max(abs(
  qr - exp(mu[2] - mu[1]) * (-log1p(-probs))^(sigma[2] - sigma[1])
)) < 1e-12)
cat("All analytical and numerical checks passed.\n")
```
